full_judgment:
This rule at the instance of the defendants namely the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh and its Secretary is directed against the judgment and decree dated 18.5.87 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1987 affirming the judgment and decree dated 11.11.86 passed by the learned Munsif 4th court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 1021 of 1985. 

 2. The plaintiff-opposite party brought the suit for declaration that the order of dismissal dated 7.8.83 issued by defendant No.2 at the instance of the defendant No.1 was illegal, inoperative, without jurisdiction, of no value in the eye of law and not binding upon the plaintiff and for a further declaration that the plaintiff is in service of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh as executive officer. 

 3. The plaintiffs case was that he was an Assistant Executive and was posted to Com ilia to start his office-cum-sale center there. On 15.2.80 he was appointed as junior executive and was transferred to Dhaka. After he joined at Dhaka the plaintiff received on 27.11.80. an order of suspension and after four- teen and a half months a charge bearing some false allegations were served on him on 11.2.82. The allegations were on three counts namely that (1) He was irregular in attending office and in opening the sale center; (2) that he purchased cycle parts and did not record the expenditure in the relevant register and lastly (3) that he spent over Taka 10,000/- on account of purchase of stationary without recording them in the register. The plaintiff submitted reply denying the allegations and claiming them to be false. The defendants appointed Mr. Moazzem Hossain, Deputy Secretary, Establishment Division who after inquiry laid a report on 10.4.82 that the charges on the count Nos. 2 and 3 were not proved but that the charge under count No.1 that is his being irregular in attending office and in opening sale centre was proved and recommended for giving him a warning. The plaintiff objected to the report pleading that the report was based on a photo copy of the attendance register which was a fabricated document whereupon the defendants after considering his representation appointed another inquiry officer namely Mr. A.K.M. Shamsuzzaman and he submitted report saying that even the charge under count No. 1 was not proved. Thus in-spite of the said report of the inquiry officer to the effect that none of the charges was proved the defendants by the impugned order illegally dismissed him from service. This violated the Government Servant's (Discipline and Appeal) Rules as also the principles of natural justice and the plaintiffs representation to the higher authorities having not been considered the plaintiff brought the suit. 

 4. The defendants contested the suit pleading that the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and was liable to be dismissed and that the suit has no merit because the plaintiff was dismissed from service after following the procedures prescribed by the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules. 

 5. The learned Munsif after considering the evidence found that the dismissal order passed by the defendants was not legal and was against the principles of natural justice and also that the suit was not barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff had prayed for consequential relief. Accordingly he decreed the suit making the declaration as was prayed adding that the plaintiff holds his service with all rights and privileges attached to his office though there was no such prayer in the suit by way of prayer for consequential relief with advalorem court fees under section 7(4)(c) of the Court Fee's Act. 

 7. Present Civil Revision is directed against the said decree. 

 9. It was next submitted that in this suit the plaintiff did not pray for any consequential relief and framed the suit as a simple declaratory suit only to seek declaration that the dismissal order was illegal and another declaration that the plaintiff is in service. So he submitted that the suit was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In support of his contention he cited the decisions reported in 3S DLR High Court Division at page 224 and B.C.R. 1988 High Court Division at page 44 besides an unreported decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 229 of 1983. 

 10. In this connection the learned Advocate also submitted that the District Judge while passing the impugned order wrongly held that the second declaration sought in the plaint namely that the plaintiff is in service amounts to consequential relief ignoring the decision of the Appellate Division which was referred to him wherein it was clearly held that a second declaration namely that the plaintiff is in service does not amount to consequential relief. 

 11. On behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate submitted at so far as the factual merit of the suit is consrned there was no scope for controversy namely .at the principles of natural justice were violated because the inquiry officer who was appointed by the defendant petitioner subsequently himself gave finding that none of the charges was proved and in such report the defendant had no legal scope to pass the order of dismissal against the plaintiff who as found innocent of the charges upon inquiry held y the defendant's officer. So to sustain such illegal order of dismissal against the employee namely the lain tiff who was innocent of the charges would amount to serious injustice and, therefore, the courts in concurrently deciding to decree the suit knitted no illegality. 

 12. On the point of maintainability of the suit Mr. Fazlul Karim submitted that from the facts indenture of the case the suit seeking declaration that the dismissal order was illegal and seeking a further declaration that the plaintiff is still in service constituted the suit as one for both declaration and for conquential relief. Mr. Fazlul Karim elaborated his arguments by further submitting that according to the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act only much relief which are necessary for the plaintiff to take and such reliefs without which the object of the suit and the purpose of the declaration is not proved are required to be sought. According to him in e present case if the plaintiffs prayers as contained I the plaint namely declaration of the dismissal order as illegal with further declaration that the plaintiff is in service will serve the whole object of the lit and, therefore, no further relief was required to sought within the meaning of the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Advocate supported the reasons given by the learned District Judge namely that a further declaration that was night for declaration that the plaintiff is in service 'as in essence a consequential relief within the leaning of the proviso. 

 "Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief; 

 Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so." 

 15. According to the said section it is a discretion of the Court to make a declaration of any status or right upon a suit being instituted by a person who is entitled to such status or right. But the section at the same time provides a positive bar that no court shall make such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so. It is to be seen what is meant by the words 'being able to seek further relief. This further relief must flow necessarily from the relief of declaration and the reliefs must be one which would complete the claim of the plaintiff and not lead to multiplicity of suits. If the relief is remote and is not connected with the cause of action then the plaintiff need not claim such relief. The further relief must be a relief which is absolutely necessary for serving the object of the suit and the purpose of the declaration. If, however, the declaration sought by it- self is sufficient to serve the object of the suit and serves fully the relief for which the cause of action for the suit arose then no further relief need be sought. But contrarily if the declaration sought by the suit itself does not serve the object of the suit and meet the purpose of the declaration then of course such further relief which willfulfill the object of the suit and declaration must be sought. For example if a plaintiff is in possession of a land he can maintain a simple suit for declaration of title without seeking any further relief like confirmation of possession as mere declaration of title serves fully the object of the suit when his title is disputed while the plaintiff is fully in possession of the land. But if a plaintiff is out of possession then his suit. for mere declaration of title without any prayer for recovery of possession is hit by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act because without having possession of the land the object of the suit will be frustrated and the declaration of title will be of no consequence. 

 16. In this connection Mr. Fazlul Karim referred to the decision of the Privy Council wherein it was held that a further proceeding may be instituted for such relief in future. The learned Advocate wanted to suggest that if after the declaration as was prayed by the plaintiff if the defendants do not reinstate him in service or give him any posting or salary, he may bring fresh suit for such relief. Mr. Fazlul Karim also argued that there was no reason for the plaintiff to presume or to apprehend that the Corporation namely the defendants will not reinstate him in service and will not pay him his wages even after such declaration is made and confirmed by the highest Court. 

 17. So far as the Privy Council decision re-ported in P.L.D. 1949 (P.C.) at page 1 is concerned it may be noted that in that case the law provided in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was not considered. But section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and its proviso clearly bars a suit in which relief which is consequential to the declaration and without which the declaration becomes meaningless and frustrates the object of the suit must be claimed in the suit and, therefore, there is no scope that such suit will be maintained leaving an opportunity to the plaintiff to bring fresh suit for the further relief which was consequential to the declaration. 

 19. So far as the present suit is concerened the plaintiff brought the suit seeking two declarations-(1) that the dismissal order passed against the plaintiff was illegal and (2) that the plaintiff is in service. Both are the reliefs of declaration as was worded in the plaint itself as also in the impugned order and decree. It was, however, sought to be interpreted by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the second declaration namely that the plaintiff is in service of Trading Corporation of Bangladesh as executive officer is a consequential relief. This contention is to be rejected outright and as a matter of fact this contention was inconsistent with the other submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim himself namely that the declaration sought was them-selves sufficient to serve fully the object of the suit and that further consequential relief by way of rein-statement in service giving posting and pay were unnecessary. In other words Mr. Fazlul Karim submitted that if the declaration sought as prayed for was made the plaintiff will automatically get his rein-statement in service, his posting and his pay and all benefits. This contention does not appear to be acceptable. No doubt according to the plaintiffs prayers in the suit both the declarations have been made by the court namely that the dismissal order is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service. But the fact remains that the plaintiff upon the dismissal has been thrown out of his office and has for all intents and purposes out of his office posting and pay. If inspite of this decree the defendants do not reinstate him in service and do not give him any posting or pay or office what benefit he will derive simply by holding a decree with a declaration that his dismissal order is illegal and he is still in service. The suit was brought with the allegation that he was illegally and vindictively dismissed from service and that inspite of his representation up to the highest authority he could not get any redress whereupon he was obliged to seek relief in the court. Now after getting a decree for declaration that the dismissal order is illegal and that he is in service this decree will not give him any benefit for which he brought the suit because by remaining out of office and out of posting his remaining at home with the declaratory decree in his pocket will serve no useful purpose of the suit and of the declaration. 

 20. The position of the plaintiff will be that he will have the declaration by the decree without any legal scope to implement it. On the other hand if along with the declaration he would have asked for a mandatory direction on the defendants to reinstate him in service with effect from the date of dismissal and to give him immediate posting and also salary then only he could get the practical benefit of the suit and the decree. So within the meaning of proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act by way of mandatory direction on the defendants to reinstate him in service with effect from the date of dismissal and posting, office and pay were the reliefs consequential to the declaration that fall within the meaning of the word 'being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title. 

 21. It is true that the decisions reported in 13 D.L.R. (H.C.) 341, 37 D.L.R. (H.C.) 7, P.L.D. 1954 (Sind) 199 and A.I.R. 1954(Bombay) 217 decided that a suit for declaration that the dismissal is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service is maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief. But the other decisions referred to from the side of the petitioner namely the decisions reported in 35 D.L.R. (H.C.) 224, B.C.R. 1988 (H.C.) 44 and an unreported decisions of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 229 of 1983 which is a judgment of affirmance of the decisions reported in 35 D.L.R.(H.C.) 224 has clearly decided that a suit for declaration that the dismissal order is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service is not maintainable and is hit by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 22. The judgment of the Appellate Division was passed in respect of O.C. Suit No. 15 of 1982 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur for declaration that the order of dismissal passed by defendant-respondent No. 1 is illegal, ultravires, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the plaintiff is still in service. The present suit is exact- y similar as it is also a suit for self same declaration. So there is no distinguishing point. 

 23. Mr. Fazlul Karim tried to draw a distinction by submitting that in the suit before the Appellate Division it was held by the courts that the dismissal order was legal while in the present suit the dismissal order was held to be illegal. The findings n the suit though different does not make any distinction regarding the framing of the suit which was exactly same. So there is no scope to give a different finding on the point of law namely about the bar of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act after the decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court which is dated 7th September, 1983. 

 24. So upon a consideration of the point of maintainability of the suit I find that the present suit was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in as much as no consequential relief was sought in the suit for declaration and that in the absence of any relief being sought for consequential relief by way of mandatory direction for reinstatement in service from the date of dismissal and for giving the plaintiff posting and salary the decree of declaration would be not only ineffective but also infructuous and of no benefit to serve the object of the suit. 

 28. Mr. Fazlul Karim referred to the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submitted that in view of the said provision as it exists now the revisional power of the High Court Division has been restricted by providing that even if any order is found to suffer from error of law that alone can not be a ground for revision unless it has occasioned a failure of justice. 

 29. Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is in the following language: 

 30. From my foregoing findings it appears that by the impugned decree an illegal order of dismissal that was passed by the defendants was declared as being not binding on the plaintiff and though this impugned order and decree suffer from error of law only on the legal ground namely that consequential relies was not sought in the suit and the declaratory decree was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but the fact remains that the said de Cree can not be held to have occasioned any failure 0 justice. If the impugned decree which suffers from error of law stands the defendants will not suffer any thing .beyond that they will not be able to reap the benefit of an illegal order passed by them and deprivation of such illegal benefit can not be said to having  occasioned failure of justice to them. In this view the matter it is held that though the impugned order suffers from error of law but they having not occasioned any failure of justice they do not call for an revision within the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
